analysis.one_liner: Tightens rules on employers of H-1B and L-1 visa workers, raising required wages, forcing public job postings, and capping visa workers at large firms.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced in April 2009 with bipartisan sponsorship, was referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee and never received a committee vote or any floor action before Congress ended in January 2011.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have rewritten the rules for two guest-worker visas used heavily in the technology industry: the H-1B "specialty occupation" visa and the L-1 intracompany transfer visa. It would have forced employers to pay visa workers at least the highest of several wage benchmarks, to post every open position publicly for 30 days so US workers could apply, and to bar ads that say a job is only for H-1B holders. It would have banned most "outsourcing" placements where a staffing firm parks a visa worker at a client company, capped visa workers at half the workforce for companies with 50 or more US employees, doubled penalties, and given the Labor Department 200 new enforcement staff plus mandatory annual audits of large visa-using employers. The bill was introduced by Senator Dick Durbin with bipartisan support and was referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee on the day it was introduced. It never received a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote before that Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: US workers in technology and other white-collar fields would gain the most: higher required wages for visa holders remove the incentive to hire an H-1B worker at below-market pay instead of an American, the 180-day displacement window protects US employees laid off around visa placements, and public job postings mean openings are actually visible to US applicants. H-1B and L-1 workers themselves also gain — wage floors, equal benefits, and anti-retaliation rules protect them from employers who use visa status as leverage.
analysis.who_benefits_short: US tech workers and visa holders

how_it_helps.text: Raises the required wage for H-1B and L-1 workers to the highest of three measures — the local prevailing wage, the median wage for the occupation, and the median skill-level-2 wage — so companies can no longer pay visa holders at the bottom of the pay scale to undercut US staff.
Doubles the protection against displacing US workers from 90 to 180 days and applies it to all H-1B employers, not just 'H-1B dependent' ones, closing a loophole big users exploited.

Caps H-1B and L-1 employees at 50% of the workforce for any US employer with 50 or more workers — aimed squarely at outsourcing and staffing firms whose business model is filling client sites with visa labor.

Bans job ads that state a position is open only to H-1B holders or that give them hiring priority, and requires each position to be posted publicly on a Labor Department website for 30 days so US workers can actually apply.

Doubles civil penalties, makes DOL audits mandatory for at least 1% of H-1B employers annually and for every large employer where visa workers exceed 15% of staff, authorizes 200 new DOL enforcement employees, and adds whistleblower-style anti-retaliation and lost-wage liability so violations carry real consequences.

analysis.who_pays: Companies that employ H-1B and L-1 workers would pay more: higher wage floors, doubled penalties, mandatory audits, and the 50% workforce cap all raise costs. IT outsourcing and staffing firms — whose model is placing visa workers at client companies — would be hit hardest, since the bill restricts exactly that arrangement. Some compliance burden would fall on legitimate users like universities and hospitals.
analysis.who_pays_short: IT outsourcing firms and large tech employers

drawbacks.text: The bill imposed no new cap on total H-1B visas but layered significant new requirements on every employer that uses them — wage floors set at the highest of three measures, 30-day public job postings, W-2 disclosure, and mandatory audits — costs an honest supporter would acknowledge fall hardest on smaller firms and on universities and hospitals that legitimately use the visas.

A good-faith objection: employers argue the H-1B program fills genuine skill shortages, and that sharply raising the wage floor and capping visa workers at 50% of a large workforce could push companies to move the work offshore entirely rather than hire US workers — which would help no American worker.

The enforcement machinery depends on appropriations: the bill authorizes 200 new Labor Department enforcement staff 'such sums as may be necessary,' but the money is not guaranteed, so the audit and investigation powers could exist on paper without the staff to use them.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For US tech workers the upside was concrete: higher wage floors, longer job-posting and displacement protections, a cap on visa-heavy workforces, and real audits instead of paper reviews, all aimed at making H-1B and L-1 hires a supplement to rather than a substitute for American workers. The costs are real but narrow: employers would pay more for visa labor and comply with audits and postings, some firms might shift work offshore rather than hire US workers, and genuine specialist shortages could be harder to fill. On balance the design targeted documented abuses — outsourced staffing arrangements, below-market wages, ads excluding US applicants — with enforcement money and penalties to match, making the benefits likely to outweigh the compliance burden. The bill's larger failure was one of design by Congress itself: with a Democratic committee and a bipartisan sponsorship, it still never got a vote, so no cost-benefit trade-off was ever tested on the floor.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee the day it was introduced, and the committee never took it up before the two-year Congress ended, so it died without a vote.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced in the Senate on April 23, 2009 and read twice before being referred to the Committee on the Judiciary the same day.
The action history shows no further action — no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, no floor vote — through the end of the 111th Congress on January 3, 2011.
The bill had bipartisan sponsorship: a Democratic lead sponsor and two cosponsors, one Republican and one Independent, yet still never advanced out of committee.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers that rely on H-1B and L-1 visa workers — especially IT outsourcing and staffing firms — are better off, because the wage floors, hiring caps, and audits never took effect.

for.name: Sen. Dick Durbin
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on April 23, 2009 and managed its referral to the Judiciary Committee.

for.name: Sen. Chuck Grassley
for.what_they_did: Joined as the Republican cosponsor; the bill was introduced 'for himself and Mr. Grassley.'

against.name: Senate Judiciary Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on the day it was introduced and took no further action on it — no hearing, no markup, no vote — for the rest of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship was bipartisan — a Democratic lead sponsor, one Republican cosponsor (Grassley of Iowa), and one Independent cosponsor — but because the bill never reached a vote, the record shows no party-split vote; the bill died in committee without either party's caucus acting on it.

industries.note: These firms staff client sites largely with H-1B and L-1 workers. The bill's 50% workforce cap, the ban on placing L-1 workers at outside client worksites for more than a year, and doubled penalties strike directly at that business model.

industries.industry: Large technology and consulting employers that use H-1B visas
industries.note: Higher wage floors, mandatory audits, public job postings, and doubled penalties raise the cost of each visa hire. Some firms would absorb that as a compliance cost; firms using the visas to hold down US wages would lose that advantage, which is the point of the bill.

industries.industry: Companies that rely on intracompany (L-1) transfers to staff US operations
industries.note: The bill adds wage and working-condition requirements, new-office documentation rules, and a report on the blanket-petition process for L-1 transfers, raising costs for multinationals moving employees into the US. Ordinary workers gain because visa workers must be paid US-scale wages.
